PHASE 4 · ADVANCED PRIMARY CARE CLINICAL MANAGEMENT

Week 81 — Lesson 105: Osteoarthritis Management

FNP-level goal: Diagnose osteoarthritis from a pattern rather than an x-ray alone, separate common degenerative joint symptoms from infection, crystal arthritis, inflammatory arthritis, fracture, and referred pain, and build a long-term plan centered on function, safety, and shared decisions.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain OA as disease of the whole joint, including cartilage, subchondral bone, synovium, ligaments, tendons, muscles, and pain processing.
  • Recognize typical OA patterns in the knee, hip, and hand while identifying features that suggest an alternate or urgent diagnosis.
  • Perform a focused joint, gait, neurologic, and functional examination and use imaging selectively.
  • Apply nonpharmacologic, pharmacologic, injection, assistive-device, and referral principles while accounting for kidney, cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, fall, and medication risks.
  • Use symptom severity, functional limitation, psychosocial context, and patient goals to decide when orthopedic, physical therapy, rheumatology, or urgent evaluation is appropriate.

Part 1 — OA Is Not Simply Wear and Tear

Osteoarthritis is a chronic disorder of the whole joint. Mechanical loading, aging, prior injury, congenital alignment, obesity, muscle weakness, occupation, genetics, and inflammatory signals can contribute. Cartilage loss matters, but so do subchondral bone remodeling, synovial inflammation, osteophytes, ligament and meniscal changes, periarticular muscle weakness, and central pain processing. This explains why x-ray severity and patient pain or disability do not always match.

FNP care should avoid two common errors: telling a patient that nothing can be done because OA is degenerative, and treating every painful x-ray finding as the cause of symptoms. The clinical goal is better function, lower symptom burden, preserved independence, and safe escalation when the pattern changes.

Part 2 — Recognizing the OA Pattern

OA pain typically worsens with use and improves with rest, although severe disease can cause rest or night pain. Morning stiffness is usually brief rather than prolonged. Knee OA may cause activity-related pain, crepitus, bony enlargement, reduced range of motion, instability, or varus or valgus alignment. Hip OA can produce groin, buttock, thigh, or even knee pain and may reduce internal rotation. Hand OA often involves bony enlargement of distal or proximal interphalangeal joints and the thumb base.

Clinical diagnosis is often possible from history and examination. Imaging is not required to prove common OA when the pattern is clear and no alternate pathology is suspected. An x-ray can be useful when diagnosis is uncertain, trauma or alternate pathology is suspected, symptoms are atypical, or surgery is being considered. MRI is not routine for established OA and may find incidental degenerative changes that do not explain pain.

Part 3 — The Joint Red Flags

Acute monoarthritis with marked warmth, swelling, restricted movement, fever, systemic illness, immunosuppression, recent procedure, bacteremia risk, or inability to bear weight must raise concern for septic arthritis. Joint infection can rapidly damage cartilage and requires urgent assessment; do not inject a hot swollen joint or assume it is OA or gout without appropriate evaluation. Crystal arthritis, hemarthrosis, fracture, inflammatory arthritis, reactive arthritis, and cellulitis are additional possibilities.

Rapid progression, unusual night pain, weight loss, history of cancer, neurologic deficit, trauma, hip pain with inability to bear weight, or pain out of proportion to examination should prompt reassessment. OA can coexist with another disease. A patient with known OA can still develop septic arthritis, fracture, DVT, radiculopathy, or inflammatory disease.

Part 4 — Focused Examination and Function

Inspect alignment, swelling, erythema, skin integrity, quadriceps or gluteal atrophy, bony enlargement, deformity, and assistive-device use. Palpate joint line and periarticular structures, assess active and passive range of motion, crepitus, stability, gait, transfers, balance, hip range, foot mechanics, and the joint above and below. Evaluate for warmth or large effusion and perform a focused neurologic and vascular examination when symptoms suggest a nonarticular cause.

Ask functional questions: Can the patient get up from a chair, walk to the mailbox, climb stairs, sleep, work, shop, care for children, exercise, or use the bathroom safely? Function and goals determine treatment intensity more reliably than x-ray wording. Screen for falls, depression, sleep disturbance, obesity stigma, food insecurity, transportation, and caregiving burdens because they affect access to activity and rehabilitation.

Part 5 — Exercise Is Foundational Treatment

Education, self-management support, exercise, weight management when appropriate and desired, and joint-protective strategies form the foundation of OA care. Exercise should be specific: strengthening supports the joint, aerobic conditioning improves endurance and cardiovascular health, and balance or neuromuscular work can improve confidence and fall risk. Aquatic, cycling, walking, tai chi, or land-based programs can be matched to the patient's ability, access, comorbidities, and preferences.

Do not tell a patient simply to lose weight or exercise more. Identify the barrier: pain flare, unsafe neighborhood, limited time, low income, fear of falling, depression, language, lack of transportation, or a misunderstanding that pain always means damage. Partner with physical therapy, community programs, and culturally relevant supports. A graded plan is more sustainable than an idealized one.

Part 6 — Symptom Treatment Requires Risk Assessment

Topical and oral medications may help selected patients, but OA pharmacotherapy is not risk-free. Before recommending an NSAID, assess kidney disease, hypertension, heart failure, coronary disease, gastrointestinal bleeding or ulcer history, anticoagulants or antiplatelets, age, pregnancy, asthma sensitivity, alcohol use, and other nephrotoxic drugs. Topical agents may reduce systemic exposure for some localized pain. Acetaminophen, duloxetine, and other options have context-specific benefits and risks; check interactions, liver disease, sedation, falls, and mental-health conditions.

Avoid routine long-term opioids for chronic OA. They rarely restore durable function and can cause sedation, falls, constipation, dependence, overdose, and interaction harm. If pain remains severe despite a well-designed conservative plan, revisit diagnosis, function, sleep, mood, activity, biomechanics, and referral options rather than escalating medication indefinitely.

Part 7 — Injections, Braces, and Devices

Intra-articular therapies can be considered for selected patients, but the indication, expected benefit, infection exclusion, diabetes implications, frequency, and procedural skill matter. A new hot swollen joint needs diagnostic thinking before injection. Braces, canes, walkers, footwear modification, splints, and occupational therapy can improve pain, stability, and safety when matched to the affected joint and patient abilities. Improper device height or a device used on the wrong side can worsen gait and falls, so teach and reassess use.

Procedural plans should be shared decisions. An injection is not a substitute for strength, conditioning, weight-neutral health support, fall prevention, or ongoing management of comorbidities. Document the goal: a family trip, ability to participate in physical therapy, safer transfers, or temporary symptom relief while waiting for a specialist.

Part 8 — When to Refer

Refer to physical therapy for individualized strengthening, gait, balance, range of motion, and home-program development. Consider orthopedic evaluation when pain and functional limitation remain substantial despite appropriate nonoperative treatment, when there is progressive deformity or instability, or when a patient wants to discuss joint replacement. The decision to refer is based on symptoms, function, risk, expectations, and readiness—not an x-ray alone.

Consider rheumatology when persistent inflammatory features, unexplained multi-joint swelling, prolonged morning stiffness, systemic symptoms, or diagnostic uncertainty suggest an inflammatory or crystal disorder. Urgent evaluation is indicated for suspected septic arthritis, acute fracture, neurovascular compromise, or inability to bear weight with concerning findings.

Part 9 — FNP Case: OA or Septic Arthritis?

A patient with known knee OA develops abrupt severe pain, fever, a hot large effusion, and inability to bear weight. The FNP does not call this an OA flare or inject the knee. Septic arthritis and crystal arthritis require urgent evaluation, including appropriate aspiration and emergency or specialty pathway. A chronic diagnosis does not protect a patient from an acute emergency.

Part 10 — FNP Case: Pain and Function Do Not Match the X-Ray

A patient has modest radiographic knee OA but cannot shop because of pain, poor sleep, fear of falling, and deconditioning. The FNP validates the disability, checks for hip, spine, neuropathic, mood, and medication contributors, then builds a graded strengthening, sleep, pain-safety, and physical-therapy plan. The x-ray is one datum, not a verdict about the patient's experience.

Part 11 — FNP Case: A Hip Problem Felt at the Knee

A 67-year-old reports persistent knee pain but has limited hip internal rotation and groin discomfort. Knee radiographs are mild. The FNP expands the examination beyond the painful location, considers hip OA or referred pain, and directs testing or therapy accordingly. Examination of the joint above and below prevents tunnel vision.

FNP High-Yield Framework: JOINT

  1. J — Judge urgency: hot swollen joint, fever, fracture, inability to bear weight, systemic illness, and neurovascular signs require escalation.
  2. O — Observe the whole joint and person: gait, alignment, hip and spine, strength, mood, sleep, falls, and function.
  3. I — Individualize imaging and medications: ask a clinical question and assess renal, GI, cardiovascular, bleeding, and interaction risk.
  4. N — Nurture function: education, strengthening, activity, devices, self-management, weight-neutral or weight-supportive care, and rehabilitation.
  5. T — Team referral: PT, OT, orthopedics, rheumatology, pain care, or urgent evaluation based on pattern and goals.

Take-Home Summary

OA is a whole-joint, whole-person condition. The FNP uses pattern recognition to diagnose typical disease, remains alert to infection and inflammatory mimics, and measures success by function and quality of life. Exercise, education, safe symptom treatment, devices, and appropriate referral can improve independence even when structural changes remain.

Educational note: This lesson supports FNP clinical reasoning and does not replace joint aspiration, imaging interpretation, procedural training, individualized medication prescribing, or rheumatology and orthopedic consultation. A hot swollen joint, fever, rapid functional decline, acute inability to bear weight, trauma, or neurovascular findings requires urgent assessment.
